To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
kerosene is affordable even to the poorest of the urban population, but electricity is too expensive for even the relatively well todo.

(1) kerosene is the cheapest energy source for the urban poor; (2) the energy ladder is a useful hypothesis for the urban areas in general, but not for the lower levels of aggregation; (3) the demand for traditional fuel is income elastic and price inelastic; (4) the cross price elasticites show that increase in price of a traditional energy source will shift demand mainly to other traditional energy sources, rather than to modern energy sources.

(i) kerosene is the most affordable energy source for the poor, (ii) electricity is the most expensive, (iii) butane gas may be affordable for the upper strata of the poor, (iv) the relevance of the 'energy ladder' hypothesis is not universal, (v) demand for traditional fuels is price elastic and (vi) demand for traditional and modern fuels is cross-price elastic.
